name: Beard growth supplements (Beardalicious, etc.)

lead: Beard growth pills are commercial supplements, typically blends of vitamins such as biotin with herbal extracts, promoted to people who want fuller, thicker facial hair.

Marketing points to individual ingredients, and products vary. No clinical studies were found for the branded products, and reference sources report no randomized trials showing biotin helps hair in healthy people.

paras: They are taken as daily pills alongside normal beard care, usually for months, since hair grows slowly. Some people combine them with minoxidil or grooming routines.
US supplements can be sold without premarket approval, and analyses cited by Wikipedia have found mislabeling or undeclared drugs in some supplement categories. Biotin can interfere with lab tests.

angle.text: Vitamin and herbal blends are promoted as feeding follicles for a thicker-looking beard. The appearance benefit is a marketing claim; published trials of these branded products were not found.

lead: Beard growth supplements are branded oral products, often vitamin or herbal blends, promoted for facial hair. In the US they are regulated as dietary supplements, which can carry structure/function claims with an FDA disclaimer but are not required to be approved before sale.[1]

Reference sources report no randomized trials showing biotin helps hair in healthy people, and that dietary supplements are generally not recommended for hair loss.[2][3] No studies found address specific branded beard supplements.

paras: Under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, supplements are treated as food; disease claims are prohibited, and labels must state that structure/function claims are not FDA-evaluated.[1] The FDA can act on unsafe products after they are marketed.[1]

Wikipedia cites a 2015 New York Attorney General review that found only about 20 percent of tested herbal supplements contained the plants on the label (method disputed), and a study that found unlisted pharmaceuticals in 776 products sold from 2007 to 2016, mostly weight-loss or sexual-performance products.[1] These figures concern supplements broadly, not beard products specifically.
Biotin at 5 mg/day or more can interfere with thyroid and vitamin D immunoassays.[2]
